catalog_quote: [Hume ROA-180 p.5] As illustrated in (4), word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Coda consonants are stress-insensitive. (4) spóu 'kind of boat' ... polí:sa 'police' ... marsína 'machine' ... kúnsi 'key' ... When words and morphemes are concatenated within an utterance, main stress falls on the rightmost morpheme with secondary stress generally occurring on alternating syllables preceding the main stress (suffixes are typically extraprosodic, however, and long vowels are always stressed). ... e. rò:nénu 'they eat turtle' f. mà:nwá:na 'chick' ... h. matrúma 'master of the house' *[màtrúma] ... While long vowels attract secondary stress, as evidenced by (5d-f), closed syllables do not. Rather, as shown in (5g-h), they pattern with monomoraic open syllables (5i-j), supporting our assumption that consonants in Leti are non-moraic. audit.reasoning: (1) Deciding quotation confirmed verbatim in the Hume ROA-180 PDF we hold at p.5 (fn.5 p.4). (2) The record formally rests on a 1997 theoretical phonology article with second-hand data, graded 'quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2', but the authoritative reference grammar by the native-speaker linguist (van Engelenhoven 2004, ch. II sec. 4.4 'Stress', p.79: 'Stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the lexical root'; codas weightless, long-vowel penults heavy; main stress on rightmost lexical root of the section) is already held by the project in the our earlier reading tree and agrees point for point with the classification (fixed penult, right edge, heavy=CVV, phrase-final main stress, buffered secondary). (3) Hume, Muller & van Engelenhoven 1997 (Phonology 14) downloaded now from the Leiden open repository, p.383, also confirms. No instrumental study is known. tone.quote: Stress and pitch are inherently linked to the nucleus of the penultimate syllable. [...] It has been explained that stress and pitch are fixed to the vowel in the penultimate syllable of the Leti lexical root. The fact that pitch and stress express prosodic prominence allows for a prosodic analysis of the Leti syllable [...] 4.7 Intonation. Among speakers of Leti there is a habit to locate one's domain or origin by the intonation pattern that is used. The four most salient intonation patterns in Tutukeian Leti are shown in the following sentence: [...] a. neutral/ unmarked intonation [...] b. topic intonation [...] c. emphatic intonation [...] d. question intonation
